findings.source_passage: So fare thee well, poor devil of a Sub-Sub, whose commentator I am. Thou belongest to that hopeless, sallow tribe which no wine of this world will ever warm
findings.source_locator: Second paragraph of source, opening of the farewell address to Sub-Sub
findings.why_it_matters: The farewell address to the Sub-Sub is one of the most tonally distinctive passages in the entire prefatory apparatus of Moby-Dick — a sustained ironic elegy combining pathos and comedy that is critically recognized as establishing Melville's narrative register. Its complete absence erases both voice and interpretive content.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the core of the Sub-Sub farewell: 'So fare thee well, poor devil of a Sub-Sub… Thou belongest to that hopeless, sallow tribe which no wine of this world will ever warm… Give it up, Sub-Subs!' and the closing heavenly image of striking 'unsplinterable glasses.'

findings.source_passage: Give it up, Sub-Subs! For by how much the more pains ye take to please the world, by so much the more shall ye for ever go thankless!
findings.source_locator: Second paragraph, midpoint of farewell address
findings.why_it_matters: This rhetorically distinctive apostrophe — with its biblical cadence and bitter irony — is a signature passage in the critical literature on Melville's relationship to his own literary labor and obscurity. Its absence is a total loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Include this line verbatim or near-verbatim in any regeneration of the Extracts segment.

findings.source_passage: here ye strike but splintered hearts together—there, ye shall strike unsplinterable glasses!
findings.why_it_matters: This closing image — the contrast between splintered hearts on earth and unsplinterable glasses in heaven — is the rhetorical climax of the Extracts preface and one of Melville's most compressed, tonally complex images. It is entirely missing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the closing line verbatim as the conclusion of the Extracts section.

findings.source_passage: this mere painstaking burrower and grub-worm of a poor devil of a Sub-Sub appears to have gone through the long Vaticans and street-stalls of the earth, picking up whatever random allusions to whales
findings.why_it_matters: The characterization of the Sub-Sub as 'burrower and grub-worm' who traverses the 'long Vaticans and street-stalls' is critically important: it frames the entire Extracts apparatus as both encyclopedic and bathetic, and establishes the epistemological irony that governs the book's relationship to cetological knowledge.
findings.suggested_fix: The Extracts preface must appear in the draft as its own section; the Sub-Sub framing paragraph should be present, including the 'Vaticans and street-stalls' and 'higgledy-piggledy whale statements' language.

findings.source_passage: grow convivial upon tears; and say to them bluntly, with full eyes and empty glasses, and in not altogether unpleasant sadness
findings.why_it_matters: This phrase — 'grow convivial upon tears… full eyes and empty glasses… not altogether unpleasant sadness' — is a signature specimen of Melville's tragicomic voice; critics cite it as an exemplar of his tonal complexity. Its erasure removes the key voice-establishing moment of the segment.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve this phrase verbatim or within one degree; it is too rhetorically distinctive to paraphrase without total loss.

summary: The draft contains none of the source segment's content — it reproduces Chapter 1 (Loomings) instead of the Extracts preface, resulting in total loss of every signature passage including the Sub-Sub characterization, the farewell apostrophe, and the closing 'unsplinterable glasses' image.
